name: Stein Danielsen
current_role: Co-founder and Chief Solutions Officer, Cognite (per conference bio)
profile: Stein Hardy Danielsen co-founded Norwegian industrial data/AI software company Cognite in 2016 with John Markus Lervik and Geir Engdahl. Cognite's Cognite Data Fusion platform contextualizes industrial (oil & gas, energy, manufacturing) data; he has overseen applications and solutions built on it.
interesting_fact: Before Cognite he was Chief Architect at Cxense, and earlier CEO of Kopek; his background spans search, real-time systems, 3D graphics and large-scale data/transaction systems.
deep_cut_fact: He worked in product development at FAST (Fast Search & Transfer), the Norwegian enterprise-search company, and is also listed as a principal at Microsoft; he holds an MSc in Computer Science from NTNU.
notes: Low public profile; rarely interviewed. media@cognite.com seen in Dec 2025 Cognite HQ release (page blocked direct fetch; seen via search). Cognite is industrial/energy-data focused, a good podcast fit. Some sources spell his name 'Danielson'.

name: Charles Yeh
profile: Charles Yeh co-founded San Francisco identity-verification company Persona with CEO Rick Song in 2018 and serves as CTO. Persona raised a $200M Series D in April 2025 (led by Founders Fund and Ribbit) at a $2B valuation, positioning itself as a 'verified identity layer' for an agentic-AI world.
interesting_fact: Yeh tracks how fraudsters use generative AI: he notes deepfakes once carried detectable traces of their root models, but mixing models has made those traces harder to find. He is most interested in where identity and payments meet, especially privacy-conscious biometrics.
deep_cut_fact: Yeh was Rick Song's roommate for three to four years before Persona. He was the one who had long wanted to start a company and pushed Song to co-found one. Early on, he personally built a custom solution for a large Japanese identity-verification customer.
notes: Low profile compared with CEO Rick Song. No published press email found. Asked to describe founder life in one word, he chose 'Fulfilling' (Visa interview).

name: David Goate
profile: Software engineer David Goate co-founded London car insurer Marshmallow in 2017 with twins Alexander and Oliver Kent-Braham and is its CTO. It began by insuring migrants and expats who were overcharged by traditional insurers. It became a unicorn in 2021 with an $85M round at a $1.25B valuation, and later raised at a higher valuation.
interesting_fact: In 2018 the startup won a trademark battle against S&P 500 giant Marsh McLennan over the name 'Marshmallow', which the British press cast as David vs. Goliath. The FT ranked it Europe's 2nd-fastest-growing company in 2023 (660% CAGR).
deep_cut_fact: Goate and the Kent-Braham twins all previously worked at digital-identity company Yoti. The company was first incorporated in 2016 as 'Twin Thinking' and was renamed Marshmallow Technology in 2017, when the team went full time working from a gym (a Virgin Active lobby).
notes: Co-CEO twins are the public faces; Goate keeps a low profile. No published press email found (press page is JS-rendered). Sources for the gym and Twin Thinking details: Wikipedia and Yahoo Finance UK (au.finance.yahoo.com/news/entrepreneurs-tech-twins-behind-marshmallow-113830484.html).

name: Neal Fachan
current_role: Co-founder (and former Chief Scientist), Qumulo. Current active role unclear; MarketScreener shows his Qumulo founder/director role ending in 2022.
profile: Systems engineer Neal Fachan co-founded Seattle scale-out file-storage company Qumulo in 2012 with fellow Isilon veterans Peter Godman and Aaron Passey, and later served as its Chief Scientist. Earlier he was a Distinguished Engineer at Isilon, where he shaped the OneFS clustered file system (Isilon was acquired by EMC), and a principal engineer at AWS.
interesting_fact: A veteran of several startups (GeekWire counted five), his résumé runs from D. E. Shaw to Google, Clustrix, Isilon and AWS before Qumulo.
deep_cut_fact: GeekWire named him a 'Geek of the Week' in Sept 2017. He studied math and computer science at the University of New Mexico and calls himself a 'serial hobbyist', with drumming and cooking among his interests.
notes: Very low public profile. No verified personal channels found, and no recent (2025-26) public activity. Best route is probably via Qumulo (qumulo.com), though he may no longer be active there. Storage and file-systems expertise is relevant to data centers.

name: Dror Davidoff
current_role: Co-founder and strategic advisor, Aqua Security (stepped down as CEO in Nov 2025)
profile: Dror Davidoff co-founded cloud-native security company Aqua Security in Ramat Gan in 2015 with CTO Amir Jerbi and was its CEO for a decade, growing it to about 450 staff, roughly $235M raised and a peak valuation of about $1B. In November 2025 he stepped back to strategic advisor, and President/CRO Mike Dube became CEO.
interesting_fact: Aqua was founded as 'Scalock' and rebranded in 2016. Jerbi said the original name 'ended up not fitting what we aim to do.'
deep_cut_fact: Before Aqua, Davidoff was EVP Sales & Business Development at database-security startup Sentrigo (joined 2008), which McAfee acquired in 2011. He then headed global sales of database security products at McAfee (Intel Security).

public_contacts.value: Look Left Marketing (Aqua's media contact on 2025 releases, e.g. Geena Pickering / Jennifer Tanner)

notes: Now an advisor, no longer running Aqua day to day, so he may have more time for a podcast. He has author pages on Dark Reading and Cloud Native Now. The PR agency was seen via a search snippet (page blocked direct fetch).

name: Jörg Kattner
current_role: Former co-founder of Gorillas (left Feb 2021). Current role not verified; an aggregator lists him as CEO of Berlin-based JoeKa UG.
profile: Jörg Kattner co-founded Berlin quick-commerce grocery startup Gorillas with CEO Kağan Sümer in 2020, joining early that year to help it scale. He left in early 2021 holding about 10%. Gorillas later reached a ~$3B valuation and was acquired by Getir in December 2022.
interesting_fact: Announcing his exit after about a year, he wrote that he was leaving 'this rocket in good hands' and looked forward to new adventures, building another company from scratch.
deep_cut_fact: He started in marketing at Rocket Internet in 2014, then ran HelloFresh's Swiss market from 2017. In 2018 he helped build HelloFreshGO, HelloFresh's in-office lunch-fridge business, and was its COO for a year.
notes: Very low profile since 2021, with no verified current venture or public channels. WikiFX article reproduces a Gründerszene report (Feb 2021). JoeKa UG and angel-investor mentions come from aggregators (siliconvalleyinvestclub, pipeseed) and are unverified.

name: Michael Carter
current_role: Co-founder and CEO, Playco (Tokyo-based instant-games company)
profile: Michael Maxwell Carter co-founded instant-games company Playco in 2020 with Zynga co-founder Justin Waldron and game producers Takeshi Otsuka and Teddy Cross. It launched with a $100M Series A (led by Josh Buckley and Sequoia) at a valuation just over $1B. Earlier he founded Game Closure, a StartX-backed HTML5 instant-games startup that raised $12M in 2012.
interesting_fact: Playco makes games that launch instantly from a link, with no download, across Facebook Instant Games, Snapchat Minis, iOS App Clips and similar platforms. Carter predicted that for mobile gaming, 'At some point, people will hit a switch.'
deep_cut_fact: Carter helped create WebSocket: in June 2008 he led the discussions that produced the first version of the protocol, and he and Ian Hickson coined the name 'WebSocket'.
notes: He met Waldron when Waldron was advising Game Closure. He works remotely (Playco execs are spread across Tokyo, Seoul, SF and LA). No published press email or verified personal accounts found. Hurun lists Playco at a $1B valuation.
